name: Blount
rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, moderate nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~$30/tCO₂ delivered over ~1167 km to Archer Daniels Midland Co.) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)

PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$227/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here

Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

caveats: Overlaps the Riddleville Dunbarton Basin saline storage basin (theoretical capacity — storage still needs a developed well + transport, not on-site).

Forestry residue here is already drawn on by existing wood-bioenergy capacity (~0.3 Mt biogenic CO₂/yr within haul range) and the Southeast wood-pellet / export industry (EIA-63C South region); the figure shown is gross recoverable residue, NOT net of this competing use, so the spare stream available to new BiCRS is lower. (Utilization is flagged, not subtracted — see methodology.)

Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Proximate geologic storage here (~95 km)
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$144/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far

caveats: Overlaps the Basal Sands - Rome Trough saline storage basin (theoretical capacity — storage still needs a developed well + transport, not on-site).

Forestry residue here is already drawn on by the Southeast wood-pellet / export industry (EIA-63C South region); the figure shown is gross recoverable residue, NOT net of this competing use, so the spare stream available to new BiCRS is lower. (Utilization is flagged, not subtracted — see methodology.)

name: Webster
anchor_facility: Domtar Paper Co Llc Hawesville Mill (pulp_paper)
rationale: Concentrated wet animal manure / biosolids, moderate nutrient status, good (low-cost) geologic storage access (~$18/tCO₂ delivered over ~314 km to Wabash Carbon Services) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.
Overlaps the Knox Group saline storage basin (theoretical capacity — storage still needs a developed well + transport, not on-site).

Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.
Overlaps the Basal Sands - Mt. Simon saline storage basin (theoretical capacity — storage still needs a developed well + transport, not on-site).

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)

Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape

Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, excess nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~$18/tCO₂ delivered over ~434 km to Archer Daniels Midland Co.) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$165/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

caveats: Forestry residue here is already drawn on by existing wood-bioenergy capacity (~0.3 Mt biogenic CO₂/yr within haul range) and the Southeast wood-pellet / export industry (EIA-63C South region); the figure shown is gross recoverable residue, NOT net of this competing use, so the spare stream available to new BiCRS is lower. (Utilization is flagged, not subtracted — see methodology.)

ranked.label: Bio-oil (pyrolysis)
pros: Modular and distributed (Charm-style roving model)
Pyrolysis densifies the carbon, so it is cheap to haul to distant wells
Returns biochar and nutrients to fields
Low durability risk
cons: Lower CDR efficiency (~45%)
Needs dry/solid biomass — not for wet feedstocks
Higher $/t than injection where storage is proximate

ranked.label: Biochar
pros: Returns nutrients to soils, improving yields
Distributed and storage-independent; simple and near-term
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~30%)
Durability and verification questions; Frontier's lower-preference pathway

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

pros: Retrofits an existing pulp & paper mill — low execution risk, near-term

Leverages existing biomass logistics + grid connection
Existing mill to retrofit: New-Indy Catawba LLC (pulp_paper)
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$117/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here

Capture capex on flue gas

name: Beaver
rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, low nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~$33/tCO₂ delivered over ~865 km to Vaulted Deep (Los Angeles)) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

name: Davis
rationale: Diffuse municipal solid waste, low nutrient status, good (low-cost) geologic storage access (~$60/tCO₂ delivered over ~274 km to Shute Creek Facility) with a retrofittable landfill anchor (Salt Lake Valley LF) -> no WtE plant in range, but a large gas-collecting landfill is: combusting its collected landfill gas and capturing the ~100%-biogenic CO2 (LFG+CCS, ~52% of the collected-gas carbon) turns a fugitive-methane source into removal. Only the captured CO2 is counted as CDR; avoided methane is a co-benefit.

ranked.label: Landfill gas + CCS
pros: Retrofits an existing landfill gas-collection system — near-term, low execution risk
Captures concentrated, ~100%-biogenic CO2 from combusted landfill gas
Energy co-product (electricity) and avoids fugitive methane (co-benefit)
Proximate geologic storage here (~22 km)
cons: Only the captured biogenic CO2 counts as removal — uncollected fugitive methane (gas collection ~75%) is a large asterisk on the claim
Dilute, variable gas stream; capture capex on a modest flue volume

ranked.label: Landfill-gas RNG + CCS
pros: Captures the near-pure CO2 already vented by landfill-gas-to-RNG upgrading — cheap capture
RNG co-product displaces fossil pipeline gas; retrofits an existing/planned RNG project
Avoids fugitive landfill methane (co-benefit)
Proximate geologic storage here (~22 km)
cons: Only the separated CO2 is removal; the RNG carbon is combusted downstream (avoidance, not CDR) — caps CDR efficiency
Depends on a gas-upgrading / RNG project being present or viable

transport_dest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations
rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, excess nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~$24/tCO₂ delivered over ~437 km to Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$218/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

ranked.label: AD + CCS
pros: Suits wet feedstock; mature technology
RNG co-product displaces fossil gas; viable offtake option
Existing anaerobic-digestion capacity within range to retrofit
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~30-44%)
Carbon is split between the RNG (fuel) and CDR streams, capping CDR
Transport to the nearest operating well is costly (~$79/tCO₂)
Geologic storage only moderately accessible — transport adds cost

name: Fond du Lac

storage_detail.nearest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations

transport_dest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations
rationale: Concentrated wet animal manure / biosolids, excess nutrient status, moderate geologic storage access (~$27/tCO₂ delivered over ~485 km to Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option (burial/biochar) or densified bio-oil.

Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
cons: Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)

PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
Removes carbon and nutrients from an over-fertilized landscape
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$241/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here

The RNG displaces fossil gas; only the separated CO2 is removal (~33% CDR efficiency), the RNG carbon being avoidance, not CDR.

ranked.label: Landfill-gas RNG + CCS
pros: Captures the near-pure CO2 already vented by landfill-gas-to-RNG upgrading — cheap capture
RNG co-product displaces fossil pipeline gas; retrofits an existing/planned RNG project
Avoids fugitive landfill methane (co-benefit)
Proximate geologic storage here (~11 km)
cons: Only the separated CO2 is removal; the RNG carbon is combusted downstream (avoidance, not CDR) — caps CDR efficiency
Depends on a gas-upgrading / RNG project being present or viable

ranked.label: Landfill gas + CCS
pros: Retrofits an existing landfill gas-collection system — near-term, low execution risk
Captures concentrated, ~100%-biogenic CO2 from combusted landfill gas
Energy co-product (electricity) and avoids fugitive methane (co-benefit)
Proximate geologic storage here (~11 km)
cons: Only the captured biogenic CO2 counts as removal — uncollected fugitive methane (gas collection ~75%) is a large asterisk on the claim
Dilute, variable gas stream; capture capex on a modest flue volume

ranked.label: Biomass burial
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Simple and low-cost; needs no geologic CO2 storage
Works for distributed biomass
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Durability still being validated (Frontier prepurchase, not offtake)
No emissions-avoiding co-product; nutrient-export risk with ag residues

ranked.label: Biochar
pros: Distributed and storage-independent; simple and near-term
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Low CDR efficiency (~30%)
Durability and verification questions; Frontier's lower-preference pathway
Returns nutrients to soils already in surplus here
